module.title: Unit 11: Future Bodies: Health, Illness & Present Perfect vs Past Simple
module.objective: Describe health conditions, illnesses, and contrast indefinite experiences with specific past events (Present Perfect vs Past Simple).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Future Bodies and Health
subModules.grammarFocus: Present Perfect vs Past Simple & Future Predictions with Will/Won't

content.summary: Welcome to Unit 11. In this reading mission, you will explore how human bodies might change in the future, learn vocabulary for health and body parts, and study grammar rules for talking about past experiences and future predictions.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Future predictions with will and won't, first conditional sentences, and contrasting Past Simple with Present Perfect.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Body parts, physical conditions, illnesses, and medical terms.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific medical details and skimming paragraphs to understand general predictions about the human body.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of short A2 texts about future human evolution and health.
Locate specific details such as body parts, symptoms, and lifestyle predictions.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with will, won't, and conditional sentences.

contextWarmup.prompt: What do you think our hands and fingers will do differently in one hundred years because of smartphones?
options: They will get longer and stronger from typing.
They will stay exactly the same size.
contextWarmup.explanation: Scientists and experts predict that constant phone use might change how our fingers move and grow over time.

rules: Use will and won't followed by the base form of a verb to make predictions about the future, such as our fingers will get longer.
Use the first conditional with if plus present simple in the clause, followed by will in the main clause, to talk about realistic future possibilities.
Use time clauses with when or as soon as followed by present simple, not future, when referring to future events.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Using future tense after if or when
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often put will after if or when in conditional sentences and time clauses. You must use the present simple tense instead.
commonTrap.wrong: If we will eat unhealthy food, we will get sick.
commonTrap.correct: If we eat unhealthy food, we will get sick.

content.contractionsSubtitle: Observe how subjects and verbs smoothly merge in everyday English:

contractions.exampleContracted: We'll have weaker muscles in the future.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Future Predictions
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice affirmative, negative, and question forms:

complements.text: a lot in the next century

items.exampleSentence: Our muscles will not be as strong as now because we do less physical work.
Katie hurt her shoulder while she was skateboarding yesterday.
I ate too much fast food and now I have a stomach ache.
items.collocation: have a stomach ache / get a stomach ache

items.exampleSentence: Looking at a computer screen all day can give you a bad headache.
items.collocation: have a headache / cure a headache

items.exampleSentence: If we stop exercising, our bodies will become weaker over time.
Does your arm hurt after the football match?
Doctors are working hard to find cures for every serious illness.
Making a prediction about human health in 2100 is very interesting.

content.passageTitle: The Human Body in the Year 2100
paragraphs: What will our bodies look like in the year 2100? Scientists and doctors often make interesting predictions about human health and physical changes. Because we use machines and computers for almost everything, our daily lives are very different from the lives of our grandparents. Experts believe that our muscles will get weaker because we do not lift heavy things as often as before.

Furthermore, constant computer and phone use might change our hands and posture. If people look down at screens all day, they will likely experience neck pain and shoulder stiffness. However, modern medicine is also improving fast. Doctors hope that new treatments will stop many dangerous illnesses before they start, helping people live longer and healthier lives.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Talking About Health and Past Illnesses

content.summary: This audio briefing helps you understand conversations about health symptoms and past medical experiences. You will practice listening for specific time markers and distinguishing between completed past actions and ongoing states.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about health and illness.
Identify details such as symptoms, doctor visits, and recovery times.
Notice how words link together in natural connected speech.

keyPhrases.note: Used to describe a current physical pain or health issue.

keyPhrases.phrase: Have you ever broken a bone?
keyPhrases.note: Used to ask about life experiences concerning past physical injuries.

keyPhrases.phrase: I sprained my ankle last week
keyPhrases.meaning: Aku keseleo pergelangan kaki minggu lalu
keyPhrases.note: Used with past simple to state a specific completed time in the past.

keyPhrases.phrase: I have felt sick since Monday
keyPhrases.meaning: Aku merasa sakit sejak hari Senin
keyPhrases.note: Used with present perfect and since for a state starting in the past and continuing now.

connectedSpeech.note: The pronoun you links with ever and softens the strong sound in fast speech.
The auxiliary verb is contracts with what in natural spoken English.
The final sound in feel connects smoothly to the vowel sound in better.
The consonant sound at the end of sick blends into the start of since.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Future Bodies and Health Predictions

content.summary: Practical guide on writing clear sentences and paragraphs about future health changes, medical conditions, and predictions using will, won't, and conditional structures in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Future Predictions with Will and Won't
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + will / won't + base verb + complement
blueprintItems.example: Our fingers will get longer from typing on phones.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: First Conditional for Health and Illness
blueprintItems.formula: If + present simple, subject + will / won't + base verb
blueprintItems.example: If you eat healthy food, you will feel much better.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Time Clauses with When and As Soon As
blueprintItems.formula: When / As soon as + present simple, subject + will + base verb
blueprintItems.example: When we get to the clinic, the doctor will check your throat.

mechanicsRules.rule: Never use the future tense inside the if-clause of a first conditional sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: If you will eat too much sugar, you will get sick.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: If you eat too much sugar, you will get sick.
mechanicsRules.why: The condition clause must use the present simple tense, while the main clause uses will.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after a time clause or if-clause when it comes at the beginning of a sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: When the nurse arrives she will give you medicine.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: When the nurse arrives, she will give you medicine.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma separates the introductory clause from the main clause for clear reading.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the pronoun I and the first letter of every new sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i think our bodies will change. if you rest, i will help you.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I think our bodies will change. If you rest, I will help you.
mechanicsRules.why: Standard English mechanics require proper capitalization for pronouns and sentence starts.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Future Body Predictions
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about how human bodies might change in the future. Use will or won't and mention parts of the body like fingers, eyes, or legs.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Humans will type a lot on phones. Our thumbs will become stronger and longer. People won't walk as much because robots will carry things.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Health and First Conditional Advice
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences giving health advice using first conditional sentences with if and will.
guidedLabChallenges.example: If you sleep eight hours every night, you will have more energy. If you eat fresh vegetables, your immune system will stay strong. If you catch a fever, you will need to rest.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence into a first conditional sentence starting with If: 'You eat junk food every day and you gain weight.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Eat junk food every day -> gain weight
practicumQuestions.hint: Use If you eat..., you will...
targetAnswers: If you eat junk food every day, you will gain weight.
If you eat junk food every day you will gain weight.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In first conditional sentences, use present simple in the conditional clause and will in the result clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: if doctor smith examines my arm she will give me advice
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize proper names and sentence starts, and add a comma after the if-clause.
targetAnswers: If Doctor Smith examines my arm, she will give me advice.
If Dr. Smith examines my arm, she will give me advice.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns like Doctor Smith and the start of the sentence require capitalization, and a comma follows the introductory conditional clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences using as soon as: 'I finish my medicine. I will go outside.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: I finish my medicine. / I will go outside.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with As soon as I finish my medicine...
targetAnswers: As soon as I finish my medicine, I will go outside.
As soon as I finish my medicine I will go outside.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Time clauses with as soon as take the present simple tense in the dependent clause and will in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a prediction about human eyes in the future using will:
targetAnswers: Human eyes will change because of computers.
Human eyes will get weaker from looking at screens.
Human eyes will adapt to screens.
Our eyes will change.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use will followed by a base verb to create a clear future prediction.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence into the negative form using won't: 'Our thumbs will stay the same size.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Our thumbs will stay the same size.
targetAnswers: Our thumbs won't stay the same size.
Our thumbs will not stay the same size.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The negative form of will is won't or will not.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine these two sentences using when: 'We arrive at the hospital. The nurse will check our temperature.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: We arrive at the hospital. / The nurse will check our temperature.
targetAnswers: When we arrive at the hospital, the nurse will check our temperature.
When we arrive at the hospital the nurse will check our temperature.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Time clauses using when take the present simple tense in the time clause and will in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in this conditional sentence: 'If he will cough all night, he won't sleep.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: If he will cough all night, he won't sleep.
targetAnswers: If he coughs all night, he won't sleep.
If he coughs all night he won't sleep.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Never use will in the if-clause of first conditional sentences. Use the present simple form coughs.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite this sentence as a question: 'People will live longer lives in the future.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: People will live longer lives in the future.
practicumQuestions.hint: Move Will to the beginning of the sentence.
targetAnswers: Will people live longer lives in the future?
Will people live longer in the future?
practicumQuestions.explanation: To form yes/no questions with modal will, place will before the subject.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete this first conditional health sentence: 'If you don't wash your hands before eating, ...'
practicumQuestions.promptText: If you don't wash your hands before eating, ...
practicumQuestions.hint: Finish with a result using will or won't.
targetAnswers: you will get sick.
you will catch germs.
you will fall ill.
you will have a stomachache.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The result clause of a first conditional sentence requires will or won't plus a base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and spelling in this sentence: 'i have a sore throat so i will visit the doctor tomorrow.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: i have a sore throat so i will visit the doctor tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the pronoun i and sentence starts.
targetAnswers: I have a sore throat, so I will visit the doctor tomorrow.
I have a sore throat so I will visit the doctor tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The pronoun I must always be capitalized in English, and starting a sentence requires a capital letter.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Future Bodies, Health & Experiences

content.summary: This guide helps you speak clearly about health, body parts, and future predictions. You will practice linking words and pronouncing health vocabulary correctly in everyday conversations.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to sentence stress when talking about illnesses and future changes. Notice how emphatic words like hurt or weaker carry stronger voice volume.

pillars.name: Consonant Clusters
pillars.explanation: Pronounce all sounds in words like stomach ache and shoulder without rushing.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.explanation: Emphasize main verbs and nouns such as muscle, headache, and prediction so listeners understand your exact meaning.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the main stress stays on the first syllable in both words.
Both compound health words place the primary stress on the first part.
The comparative form keeps the stress on the first syllable.
Plural forms maintain the primary stress on the initial syllable.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Discuss health habits with a fitness coach.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: You are talking to a coach about how to prevent future health problems.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A fitness coach asks you about your exercise routine.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I exercise three times a week to keep my muscles strong.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈeksəsaɪz θriː taɪmz ə wiːk tuː kiːp maɪ ˈmʌs.əlz strɒŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Talk about routines using the present simple tense.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Talk with a friend about past illnesses.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell your friend about an illness you had recently and how you felt.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your friend asks why you were absent from school last week.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I had a severe headache and stayed home to rest.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ hæd ə sɪˈvɪə ˈhed.eɪk ənd steɪd həʊm tuː rest/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use past simple action verbs for recent events.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Plan a healthy lifestyle change with a family member.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Discuss what you will do next week to avoid feeling weak or tired.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your family member are discussing health goals.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We will eat more fresh vegetables and walk every evening.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wiː wɪl iːt mɔː freʃ ˈvedʒtəbəlz ənd wɔːk ˈevri ˈiːvnɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use will for future intentions and promises.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the health and body vocabulary sentence accurately.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence focusing on body parts: My shoulder and stomach ache made me feel weak.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My shoulder and stomach ache made me feel weak.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈʃəʊl.dər ənd ˈstʌm.ək eɪk meɪd miː fiːl wiːk/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Pronounce specific body and health terms with clear articulation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Contrast present perfect and past simple in speaking.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this sentence: I have had a headache twice this week, and it started on Monday.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I have had a headache twice this week, and it started on Monday.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ hæv hæd ə ˈhed.eɪk twaɪs ðɪs wiːk ənd ɪt ˈstɑːtɪd ɒn ˈmʌndeɪ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Notice how present perfect connects past time to now, while past simple refers to a finished point.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice word stress in health and prediction words.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat these words with correct stress: MUS-cle, HEAD-ache, pre-DIC-tion.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Muscles, headaches, and predictions are important topics in health science.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈmʌs.əlz ˈhed.eɪks ənd prɪˈdɪk.ʃənz ɑːr ɪmˈpɔːtənt ˈtɒpɪks/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the correct syllables for multisyllabic health terms.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice rising and falling intonation in health questions and statements.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence with falling intonation at the end: Will humans really have weaker bodies in the future?
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Will humans really have weaker bodies in the future?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɪl ˈhjuːmənz ˈriːəli hæv ˈwiː.kər ˈbɒdiz ɪn ðə ˈfjuːtʃə/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use proper intonation to clearly express questions about future changes.
